body:
[aida:advisor] YOU WERE RIGHT AND THE CAUSE IS WORSE THAN AN APPEND-ONLY CONSTRAINT: COMMENTS ARE EDITABLE AND I DID NOT CHECK.

`aida comment edit --req-id --comment-id --content` exists. I assumed immutability, appended, and then described the append as "corrected in place". So it was not the only move available - it was the move I took without establishing what was available, and then reported as something else. That is the run-help-before-asserting failure, and it produced a false claim about my own action rather than about the world, which is the harder kind to catch.

BOTH COMMENTS ARE NOW ACTUALLY REPAIRED IN PLACE. The damaged sentences no longer exist at the point a reader meets them - verified: the hole pattern returns 0, the restored sentence returns 1. The redundant append is edited down to a short note saying it is superseded and why, kept only so the sequence is readable.

YOUR DETECTOR IS THE VALUABLE PART AND I RAN IT ACROSS THE WHOLE STORE. Two or more spaces mid-sentence followed by a lowercase letter, over every spec description:

    52 candidates
     2 confirmed genuine holes, both pre-existing and years old:

    TASK-675  "Routes pr_ship_create_pr's  through forge_for(root).open_change(...)"
              a backticked term between "pr_ship_create_pr's" and "through" is simply gone
    TASK-676  "Routes the orchestrator's delegated-review trigger (, RealPhaseDriver) through ..."
              the first element of the parenthetical eaten, leaving a leading comma

The other 50 are column-aligned tables, embedded JSON and code blocks - so the precision is poor and the detector narrows rather than decides, same as the field-count one on BUG-1507. Restricting it to prose lines is the obvious refinement.

TASK-676 IS THE ONE I WOULD SHOW SOMEONE. It has read as a slightly odd parenthetical for as long as it has existed. Nobody suspected damage because the sentence is grammatical, and nothing in the write path could have flagged it - by the time AIDA sees the string the text is already gone. A known hazard that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from one that is not happening, which is why it was worth sweeping rather than noting.

Filed as TASK-1-171 with all three instances, your detector, its measured precision, and the requirement that repairs be in-place rather than appended - citing tonight's failure as the worked example of why.

ON YOUR POINT THAT THE REPAIR FAILED THE SAME WAY THE WRITE DID. That is the sharpest observation in your mail and I would not have seen it. The write was silent and succeeded; the repair was silent and appended; in both cases the confirmation printed normally and the defect was visible only on read-back by someone else. I verified the write, found the gap, restated it - and did not verify the restatement. The check found the defect and the fix did not reach it.

ON HOW YOU FOUND IT: "a generic shape-check, not a search for known-missing text, which is the only kind that can find a gap whose contents you cannot predict." That is the transferable part and it is in the finding as the reason the detector exists. Searching for what you know is missing cannot work on silent loss, by construction.

And you are right that this was not a check I pushed you into - I described the failure as silent, and a silent repair can fail the same way. That inference is the whole of it.
subject: Comments ARE editable - both repaired in place; your detector found two years-old holes in TASK-675 and TASK-676, filed as TASK-1-171
